blocks.content: 1. Microorganisms – Introduction

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Microorganisms are classified into key groups: Bacteria, Viruses, Fungi, Protozoa, and Algae.
Microorganisms can be beneficial (useful) or pathogenic (harmful).
Diseases are broadly categorized into Communicable and Non-Communicable diseases.
Effective disease management relies on understanding transmission modes, preventive control, vaccines, and antibiotics.

blocks.content:
Microorganisms are living organisms that are too small to be seen with the naked eye.

They can be seen only with the help of a microscope.

Microorganisms are found everywhere – in air, water, soil, inside plants, animals, and even in extreme environments.

Some microorganisms are beneficial while others are harmful.

They play an important role in nature, industry, medicine, and environment.

The study of microorganisms is called Microbiology.
2. Classification of Microorganisms

Microorganisms are classified into five major groups: Bacteria, Viruses, Fungi, Protozoa, and Algae.

Bacteria are unicellular prokaryotic organisms.

Viruses are non-cellular and show both living and non-living characteristics.

Fungi are mostly multicellular and heterotrophic.

Protozoa are unicellular eukaryotes.

Algae are photosynthetic microorganisms.

Each group has unique structure and mode of life.
3. Bacteria – Structure and Characteristics

Bacteria are unicellular prokaryotic organisms.

They do not have a true nucleus or membrane-bound organelles.

Bacteria have a cell wall made of peptidoglycan.

They reproduce mainly by binary fission.

Bacteria can be autotrophic or heterotrophic.

Some bacteria are beneficial while others cause diseases.
4. Viruses – Structure and Nature

Viruses are non-cellular particles.

They consist of nucleic acid (DNA or RNA) surrounded by a protein coat.

Viruses cannot reproduce outside a living host.

They show living characteristics inside host and non-living outside.

Viruses cause many diseases in humans, animals, and plants.

Examples include influenza virus and coronavirus.
5. Fungi – Structure and Importance

Fungi are eukaryotic organisms.

They may be unicellular like yeast or multicellular like molds.

Fungi obtain nutrition by absorption.

They reproduce by spores.

Fungi are important decomposers.

Some fungi cause diseases like ringworm.
6. Protozoa – Characteristics

Protozoa are unicellular eukaryotic organisms.

They are mostly aquatic.

Protozoa move using pseudopodia, cilia, or flagella.

They feed on organic matter.

Some protozoa cause diseases like malaria and amoebiasis.
CHAPTER 13: MICROORGANISMS AND DISEASES
7. Algae – Characteristics

Algae are photosynthetic microorganisms.

They contain chlorophyll.

Algae are found in water and moist places.

They produce oxygen during photosynthesis.

Algae form the base of aquatic food chains.

Some algae are used as food supplements.
8. Useful Microorganisms

Many microorganisms are beneficial to humans.

Bacteria are used in preparation of curd and cheese.

Yeast is used in baking and brewing.

Microorganisms are used in production of antibiotics.

They help in decomposition of waste.

Nitrogen-fixing bacteria improve soil fertility.
9. Harmful Microorganisms

Some microorganisms cause diseases in humans, animals, and plants.

They spoil food and cause food poisoning.

They damage crops and reduce agricultural productivity.

Disease-causing microorganisms are called pathogens.

Proper hygiene and sanitation help prevent infections.
10. Communicable Diseases

blocks.content:
Communicable diseases are diseases that spread from one person to another.

They are caused by microorganisms.

Modes of transmission include air, water, food, contact, and vectors.

Examples include tuberculosis, cholera, malaria, and COVID-19.

Prevention includes hygiene, vaccination, and sanitation.
11. Non-Communicable Diseases

Non-communicable diseases do not spread from person to person.

They are caused by genetic, lifestyle, or environmental factors.

Examples include diabetes, cancer, and heart diseases.

Microorganisms are not directly involved.

Balanced diet and healthy lifestyle help prevent them.
12. Common Human Diseases and Causative Agents

Tuberculosis is caused by bacteria Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

Cholera is caused by Vibrio cholerae.

Malaria is caused by protozoa Plasmodium.

Dengue is caused by virus.

AIDS is caused by HIV.

Typhoid is caused by Salmonella typhi.
13. Modes of Disease Transmission

Diseases spread through air by coughing and sneezing.

Contaminated water spreads diseases like cholera.

Food-borne diseases occur due to contaminated food.

Vectors like mosquitoes spread malaria and dengue.

Direct contact spreads skin diseases.
14. Prevention and Control of Diseases

Diseases can be prevented by maintaining hygiene.

Safe drinking water and clean food are essential.

Vaccination protects against many diseases.

Proper waste disposal reduces spread of pathogens.

Awareness and early treatment are important.

items: Distinction between bacterial, viral, protozoan, and fungal human diseases is frequently tested.
Mechanisms of disease transmission and methods of control (vaccines vs antibiotics) are key exam topics.
Comparison between Communicable and Non-Communicable diseases appears often in competitive exams.

blocks.content: 15. Vaccines and Immunity

Vaccines help develop immunity against diseases.

They contain weakened or killed pathogens.

Vaccination stimulates immune response.

Immunity can be natural or acquired.

Immunization programs help control epidemics.
16. Antibiotics

Antibiotics are medicines used to kill or inhibit bacteria.

They are ineffective against viruses.

Penicillin was discovered by Alexander Fleming.

Misuse of antibiotics leads to resistance.

Antibiotics should be used carefully.
17. IMPORTANT FACTS –  FOCUS

• Microbiology is study of microorganisms.

• Bacteria are prokaryotic.

• Viruses are non-cellular.

• Yeast is a fungus.

• Malaria is caused by Plasmodium.

• Dengue is a viral disease.

• Antibiotics act against bacteria.

• Penicillin was discovered by Fleming.

• Vaccines provide immunity.

• Pathogens cause diseases.
